script.speaker: Organiser
script.text: The walk is for people who want a short route with time to look at the landscape. I can take your details and go through the arrangements.

script.speaker: Walker
script.text: All right. Let’s go through the details.

script.speaker: Walker
script.text: What should I write for the route name?

script.speaker: Organiser
script.text: We are doing the Brook Loop. The longer ridge route will take place next month.

script.speaker: Walker
script.text: And what is the meeting day?

script.speaker: Organiser
script.text: Meet on Sunday. Saturday is the day the leaders check the paths.

script.speaker: Walker
script.text: Could you confirm the meeting time?

script.speaker: Organiser
script.text: The meeting time is 8:40. That is twenty minutes before nine, so there is time to check everyone’s details.

script.speaker: Walker
script.text: What have you put down for the landmark at meeting point?

script.speaker: Organiser
script.text: Meet beside the bridge. Do not wait at the nearby car park, as the two places are not visible from one another.

script.speaker: Walker
script.text: What should I write for the leader’s surname?

script.speaker: Organiser
script.text: The leader’s surname is Finch. Look for that name on the group list.

script.speaker: Walker
script.text: And what is the maximum group size?

script.speaker: Organiser
script.text: We have a limit of twelve walkers. The narrow part of the route is easier to manage with a small group.

script.speaker: Walker
script.text: Could you confirm the drink to carry?

script.speaker: Organiser
script.text: Bring water for the walk. The only café is at the end of the route.

script.speaker: Walker
script.text: What have you put down for the map colour?

script.speaker: Organiser
script.text: Your route is marked in red. The green route crosses ours but takes a different way back.

script.speaker: Walker
script.text: What should I write for the planned rest point?

script.speaker: Organiser
script.text: The rest is in the meadow. We will pass the woodland shelter before then but will not stop there.

script.speaker: Walker
script.text: And what is the return transport?

script.speaker: Organiser
script.text: A minibus will take the group back to the starting point. We have booked it for the end of the walk.

script.speaker: Organiser
script.text: Bring the confirmation with you. If the meeting point changes because of weather, we will send a message that morning.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The craft centre has four demonstration areas around the central junction. North is at the top of your plan. You can visit any two areas before the group leaves.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The printing room is west of the junction, behind the door on the left. You can watch a short run from the viewing area.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The weaving room is south of the junction. Follow the path towards the bottom of the plan and look through the wide window.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The dye garden lies east of the junction, on the right. The plants are grouped beside the outside path.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The repair bench is north of the junction, at the top of the plan. It is in the quietest corner.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The sample uses thick paper so that it holds its shape while the ink dries.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: You can feel a piece of wool from the weaving demonstration. Leave the finished cloth on its stand.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Look for the label on each pot. It gives the plant name, but you can also ask the gardener about its use.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Leave unfinished samples on the tray near the bench. We do not want small pieces to be lost in bags.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The afternoon talk starts at three o’clock. It takes place after the first two demonstrations.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Use the gate beside the main building to leave. The path through the garden ends at a locked door.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Please return to the junction when you finish. The guide will check that everyone has made it back before the outside gate is closed.

script.speaker: Leo
script.text: We will compare how much light reaches the work surfaces in two rooms. Let’s keep the observation simple enough to repeat if the first result is unclear.

script.speaker: Mina
script.text: All right. Let’s go through the details.

script.speaker: Leo
script.text: Start at desk height. A reading at the ceiling would not describe the work surface, and we are not examining floor lighting.

script.speaker: Mina
script.text: Use the slot just before lunch for both rooms. The afternoon is not available, and a morning comparison would require a different booking.

script.speaker: Leo
script.text: Record whether the blinds are open. The colour of the chairs is not a useful description of the lighting conditions.

script.speaker: Mina
script.text: Leo will borrow the light meter from the technician. Mina will prepare the map and Vic will reserve the time.

script.speaker: Leo
script.text: Mina will draw the room map and label the desks. It will be easier to match readings with locations later.

script.speaker: Mina
script.text: Vic will reserve the measurement slot for both rooms. Ask for access a few minutes before the actual observation.

script.speaker: Leo
script.text: Use a sticker on the floor to mark the position. That way the stand can be moved out and replaced accurately.

script.speaker: Mina
script.text: Take three readings at each desk, with a short pause between them. Note any large difference instead of hiding it in the average.

script.speaker: Leo
script.text: Keep the same setting on the meter throughout. We can record changes separately if the range is not suitable.

script.speaker: Mina
script.text: Enter the readings in a shared table. Put the desk code and the time next to every number.

script.speaker: Leo
script.text: Remember to record what was happening around the room. A single number will be much easier to interpret when we know where it came from.

sections.title: What a window changes about incoming light

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: A window can do more than increase the amount of light in a room. Its position and surface can also affect where the light reaches and how clearly objects can be seen.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Take a reference reading outside the window before moving the instrument into the room.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: A layer of frost on the glass can scatter light. A bright patch may then have a less distinct edge.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Move the test card along a straight line on the desk. This gives a series of readings at different distances.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Place a dark background behind the card if the patch is hard to see. Keep it in place during the comparison.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Mark the edge with a removable strip. We need to be able to change the mark when the conditions change.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Keep the card at the same angle. Tilting it could change the amount of light falling on the surface.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Compare the clear pane with a sample of frosted glass. This lets you observe a change in the pattern of light.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: As the sun changes position, the brightest region can shift across the desk. This is why we record the time.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Write down whether the sky was cloudy. A reading taken under a cloud can differ from one taken in direct sun.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Take the last photograph from the doorway. It will show the relation between the bright area and the rest of the room.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: When you finish, describe the location, the window and the condition of the sky. Those details will help another class understand the pattern you found.
